newsitem.title: USA: Ex-BankBoston CEO, cites leaks, objects to board.
newsitem.headline: Ex-BankBoston CEO, cites leaks, objects to board.

text.p: Bank of Boston's former chief executive raised the issue of leaks from the boardroom at BankBoston shareholders' meeting on Thursday.

Ira Stepanian, who abruptly resigned in July 1995 after word of a possible merger with CoreStates Financial Corp was leaked to the press, demanded to know if the person who leaked the information had been found and what was being done about it almost two years after the deal fell apart.

Stepanian said he was bringing the matter up now, as shareholders prepared to re-elect the board, because that individual had not been identified and shareholders were assured last year that the investigation was continuing.
"Nearly two years have past and we have not heard anything further," he said.

BankBoston CEO Chad Gifford, who served as president and chief operating officer under Stepanian, said the board "had discussions on the subject of possible leaks with professionals as to what must be done...We did what we should have done."
Stepanian later told reporters he was concerned about information leaking out of the board room.
"No company should be held hostage to the possibility that a director might be leaking information," Stepanian said.
Gifford told Reuters later: "That's history. It's a concern of any company. That was 22 months ago. The board discussed it and the board did what was appropriate."

Stepanian was unable to merge then Bank of Boston with either CoreStates, Mellon Bank Corp or Banc One Corp. About a year after Gifford assumed the CEO slot, Bank of Boston merged with BayBanks. Shareholders Thursday formally approved the new name, BankBoston Corp. The institution, which had assets of $64.8 billion as of March 31, is the 15th largest U.S. bank holding company.
